clue.text: Start to survey papers inside facility in holiday area

blocks.note: 'Start to' asks for the first letter of survey
facility means ease — the knack of doing something without effort
your papers are your ID, and they go inside EASE

explanation.walkthrough: 'Facility' is the trap: not a building but the noun ease. Papers for ID is a convention you will meet most weeks, and the surface is busy pretending to be a hotel inspection.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage the seaside is the coast thought of as a resort — piers, deckchairs and boarding houses — rather than the shoreline as geography.

clue.text: Russian neighbour shuffling in seat holding nothing

blocks.note: the letters of IN SEAT shuffled, with the O of 'nothing' held among them

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is the letter O — the single most useful equivalence in the game. The surface sells you a restless passenger so that 'shuffling' reads as fidgeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonia shares a long land border with Russia, so the clue defines it by example: one of several countries that would answer to the phrase.

clue.text: Conclude in this way, reportedly, ahead

blocks.note: 'in this way' is SO
to be up in a match is to be ahead in it

explanation.walkthrough: A homophone is the one device where the letters on the page are deliberately the wrong ones: you hear SO and you write SEW.
explanation.definitionFit: To sew up a deal is to settle it beyond reopening — the tailor's last seam borrowed as a picture of finishing something off.

clue.text: Put down disbandment of top side

blocks.note: the letters of TOP SIDE, broken up by 'disbandment of'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Disbandment' does the shuffling while the surface talks football: a top side being broken up is exactly the sentence a sports page would print.
explanation.definitionFit: To deposit something is to set it down and leave it there — a coat, a payment at the bank, or the silt a river drops on its bed.

clue.text: Dejection sadly about island in Middle East

blocks.note: ME is the standard abbreviation for the Middle East — the outer wrapper
alas is how you say sadly in one word, and it sits inside ME
I = island, as printed on a chart, and it goes inside ALAS

explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nested one in the other, and both wrappers are abbreviations worth banking: I for island on any map, ME for the Middle East on any news desk.
explanation.definitionFit: Malaise is a low, sapping unease you feel in the body as much as the mood, which is why doctors and political columnists both reach for it.

clue.text: Advantages when with groups

blocks.note: as and when are interchangeable — 'as I arrived'
a set is a group of things collected together

explanation.walkthrough: Two very ordinary words doing wordplay duty, which is what makes the join hard to see: nothing in the surface announces that a seam runs through it.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is anything that counts in your favour — on a balance sheet or in a team — so the definition names them by what having them buys you.

clue.text: Parts teen misused currently

blocks.note: the nine letters of PARTS TEEN, rearranged by 'misused'

explanation.walkthrough: The (2,7) enumeration is the tell: a nine-letter answer breaking after two letters is nearly always a short phrase, which narrows the guessing enormously.
explanation.definitionFit: 'At present' is the adverbial phrase for right now, so it drops straight into a sentence wherever 'currently' would stand.

clue.text: Separate soldiers captivated by dark-coloured beer

blocks.note: stout is the black beer, and it is doing the captivating
OR is Other Ranks, the army's non-officers

explanation.walkthrough: OR for Other Ranks is one of the few military abbreviations that earns its keep in crosswords. 'Captivated by' is a capture, not a compliment.
explanation.definitionFit: To sort things out is to divide them into their proper piles — the literal laundry sense, before the phrase drifted into meaning 'fix'.

clue.text: Sister, say, in a bolder violet when dressed

blocks.note: thirteen letters of A BOLDER VIOLET, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is the little flag that says you are being given one example rather than a synonym. 'When dressed' shuffles the letters while the surface arranges flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A sister is one instance of a blood relative — kin by birth rather than by marriage — and 'say' admits that cousins and uncles would do as well.

clue.text: Some paste with dish cooked in liquid

blocks.note: the answer runs across the gap: paSTE With

explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' is the standing signal to take only part of what follows, and the answer straddles two words, which is exactly where the eye refuses to look.
explanation.definitionFit: A stew is meat and vegetables simmered slowly in their own broth, so the definition names it by its method — the thing that separates it from a roast.

clue.text: Eastern Europeans given a role with nothing in common?

blocks.note: Poles are the people of Poland
an actor's role is a part, so 'a role' is A PART

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the Poles of the first half become the poles of the globe in the answer, and the space quietly moves one letter to the left.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things poles apart are as far from each other as the north and south poles, the greatest distance the earth offers — hence no shared ground at all.

clue.text: In retreat, secures edges of estuaries for wading birds

blocks.note: secures = PINS, turned round by 'In retreat'
the edges of the word, its first and last letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Secures' is the noun-verb trap: it means fastens with pins, and PINS is what gets turned round. An across entry can only retreat to the left.
explanation.definitionFit: Snipe are long-billed birds that feed by probing soft mud at the water's edge, which is what places them among the waders alongside curlews and godwits.

clue.text: Unprepared husband? Hope not somehow when touring

blocks.note: seven letters of HOPE NOT, rearranged
H is the register's abbreviation for husband, and it tours into the middle

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark after 'husband' is the setter smiling at his own surface, where a wife is doubting one. H for husband comes straight from the family tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Catch someone on the hop and you catch them off guard: the phrase pictures a person mid-skip, one foot in the air and no way to react.

clue.text: Required money with a rightwinger

blocks.note: M is the standard shorthand for money, as in the money supply
with is being used as a word meaning and, not as joinery
the clue's own a
a Tory is the British right-winger of choice

explanation.walkthrough: Four pieces in five words, and the sting is 'with': everywhere else in the puzzle it would just be glue, and here it is three letters of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mandatory is demanded by rule rather than merely expected — compulsory, the way a court order or a uniform policy is.

clue.text: Rebel is with team among Dutch conservationists

blocks.note: D is the language code for Dutch
the clue's own is, taken at face value
a side is a team in every British sports report
the National Trust, the crossword's usual conservationists

explanation.walkthrough: Both outer pieces are abbreviations rather than words, which is why the clue reads so smoothly: nothing in the surface admits that D and NT are letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A dissident is someone who publicly refuses to go along with the regime they live under, so 'rebel' names the stance rather than any uprising.

clue.text: Attractive with no end of colour – and lacking in weight?

blocks.note: attractive = pretty, about to lose a letter
the end of the word colour is R — that is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of colour' is asking for the last letter of the word itself, not for a shade. The dash marks where the wordplay stops and the definition begins.
explanation.definitionFit: A petty objection carries no weight — it is trivial, too slight to matter — and the question mark concedes that the weighing here is figurative.

clue.text: Break odd parts of some tree

blocks.note: the odd letters of sOmE, first and third
the ash is a tree

explanation.walkthrough: ASH belongs with ELM and YEW in the small set of trees setters keep to hand. 'Some' is being taken apart letter by letter rather than meaning 'a few'.
explanation.definitionFit: To smash something is to break it violently into pieces, so 'break' is the same act with the noise and the force taken out of it.

clue.text: Stonework making mother and child really discontented

blocks.note: ma is mother, informally
a son is one sort of child
the word loses its contents and keeps only its outside letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Discontented' is the elegant one here: a word emptied of its contents keeps only its outside letters. Its cousins do the same job — hollow, gutted, heartless, empty.
explanation.definitionFit: Masonry is what a mason builds — stone cut, laid and mortared into a wall — so the definition names the finished work by its material.

clue.text: Tell niece to move customers

definitions.note: Clientele is a collective singular — one body made up of many people — so the plural definition names the members while the answer names the group they form.

blocks.note: the nine letters of TELL NIECE, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'To move' works both ways at once: on the surface it is persuading a relative to shift house, and underneath it is the instruction to rearrange letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A clientele is the whole body of people who regularly buy from a business or use a professional, so the definition points at its members.

clue.text: Overlooks poor grounds?

blocks.note: to excuse a lapse is to overlook it — the verb reading
the reasons people offer for a failure — the noun reading

explanation.walkthrough: Four words, no indicators, and the split falls after the first one. The question mark is doing the work of admitting that not every excuse is a poor one.
explanation.definitionFit: To excuse a fault is to overlook it, and excuses in the plural are the feeble reasons offered for one — the verb forgives, the noun is what gets offered.

clue.text: Employee lately is taken in by enticement for free time

blocks.note: an enticement is a lure, and it does the taking in
'lately' asks for the last letter of Employee
the clue's own is, following the E inside the lure

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lately' is asking for a last letter, not telling you when — the sort of double life a short adverb leads. The whole surface reads like an HR memo.
explanation.definitionFit: Leisure is the stretch of the day left over once work and duty are done, which is precisely the everyday phrase in the definition.

clue.text: Hold up thing put on table to catch small chicken

blocks.note: a mat is what goes on the table under a hot dish
to nab someone is to catch them

explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'hold up' can only mean stand the whole assembly on its head, since there is no left or right on a vertical entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A bantam is a miniature breed of domestic fowl kept for show and eggs — the same smallness that gave bantamweight boxing its name.

clue.text: One with ambition managed to enter a second underground area

blocks.note: the clue's own a
s is the abbreviation for second, as on a stopwatch
a pit is an underground working, and it takes the insertion
to manage a business is to run it — this goes inside the pit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Managed' is past tense because RAN has to be, which is the kind of small agreement that confirms a parse. The surface is quietly about the Tube.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspirant is someone reaching for a post or a title not yet held, so the definition names them by the reaching rather than by any achievement.

clue.text: Plain-spoken person standing for election ignoring latest trio of characters

blocks.note: someone standing for election is a candidate
the last three letters of CANDIDATE — the part that is ignored

explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' means letters here rather than people, which is the whole disguise: the surface is about a politician and the mechanism is about spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone candid says what they actually think without softening it, which is what 'plain-spoken' describes — frankness rather than simple language.

clue.text: Female has partly written a diary

blocks.note: the name spans three words: writteN A DIAry

explanation.walkthrough: 'Partly' is the hidden-word flag. A name straddling three words is the hardest kind to spot, because the eye reads the words and not the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Nadia is a woman's given name, Russian in origin and familiar from the gymnast Comaneci, so the clue defines it by example rather than by meaning.

clue.text: Invest in reforms to cover case for change as things to spur people

blocks.note: eight letters of INVEST IN, rearranged by 'reforms'
the case of the word change is its outer letters, C and E

explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' asks for the outside letters of the word beside it, the way a case encloses whatever it holds. The surface is a perfectly plausible line about company finance.
explanation.definitionFit: An incentive is a reward dangled to make somebody act — a bonus, a discount, a tax break — so the definition describes them by the job they do.

clue.text: Daughter is given peculiar percussion instrument

blocks.note: D is the family-tree abbreviation for daughter
rum meaning odd, as in 'a rum do'

explanation.walkthrough: Rum for peculiar is Victorian slang that now survives almost entirely inside crosswords, so it is worth learning the moment you meet it.
explanation.definitionFit: A drum is the skin-and-shell instrument you strike rather than blow or bow, which is exactly what puts it in the percussion section.

clue.text: Sally after vacation checks organised schemes

blocks.note: vacated, the name keeps only its outer letters
to stem something is to check it, as in stemming a flow

explanation.walkthrough: Two traps in five words: 'vacation' means a word emptied out rather than a holiday, and 'checks' wants the sense of halting rather than anything on a bank counter.
explanation.definitionFit: A system is a set of parts or procedures deliberately arranged to work together, so the definition catches both the plan and the order inside it.

clue.text: Prisoner on the loose in cloak in eastern Kent area

blocks.note: E = eastern, as on any compass
Kent sits in the South East, SE on an address — and it is split open
a cape is a cloak, and it goes into the gap in SE

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wrapper are map abbreviations, which is why the clue reads like a police bulletin rather than like wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapee is anyone who has got clear of custody, so the definition describes the answer by the situation the person is now in.
